newsitem.title: USA: UK economic outlook best for a generation - Clarke.
newsitem.headline: UK economic outlook best for a generation - Clarke.

text.p: WASHINGTON, Oct 1 (Reuter) The prospects for the British economy are the best for a generation, Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke said on Tuesday.
He was speaking to the annual meeting of the IMF and World Bank only days after the 20th anniversary of when Britain had to borrow from the Fund.

"This ironic anniversary is the best evidence of the scale of the reform of the British economy over the last two decades. The recovery has broken the mould of previous British recoveries," Clarke said.
"I firmly believe that these are the healthiest set of economic prospects we in Britain have seen in a generation."
"With continued good economic management, this recovery could be the healthiest, the strongest and the longest ever enjoyed," Clarke said.

Clarke has insisted that his ruling Conservative Party will win the next general election -- which must be held by May -- on the basis of the economic recovery and that he will not tinker with it now just to pick up votes.

The party is lagging far behind in opinion polls from the Labour Party which this week is holding its annual conference in Britain and where on Tuesday it announced it would re-nationalise the country's railways.
"The answer to our success lies in the...government's far-reaching programme of structural reform over the past 17 years.
"Our agenda of privatisations, deregulation and labour market reform has made the UK economy more flexible, more responsive to changes in market conditions and less inflation-prone," he added.
This time there was a faster fall in employment, exports were growing faster than imports, there were no signs of inflationary pressure and earnings growth was half the rate of the 1980s.
"We have said we will bring inflation down to 2-1/2 percent or less, and we will," he said.

Referring to his budget, which will be set next month, Clarke said his overriding aim would be to get government borrowing down to a sustainable level and keep the country on course towards a balanced budget.
"That is the background against which I shall then judge whether or not the government can make progress in its tax-cutting agenda," he said.
"The British government believes in tax cuts but only when we can afford them, and only when they make economic good sense." REUTER
